fetched_contents.text: Every Atom Now Counts In Advanced Chip Manufacturing Artificial-intelligence workloads are pushing semiconductor design to a point where traditional scaling strategies are running out of room. Performance improvements that once came from shrinking transistors now depend increasingly on how devices are stacked, interconnected, and isolated. Transistor scaling still matters, but advanced device architectures no longer can accommodate the power density and bandwidth demands of multi-kilowatt AI systems. The result is a deeper dependence on materials that must maintain electrical, mechanical, and chemical stability under increasingly extreme conditions. Thin-film dielectrics, conformal metal barriers, and atomic-scale interfaces now play an active role in determining power efficiency, signal integrity, and long-term reliability. As AI accelerators expand in size and complexity, these films are forced to perform across more aggressive aspect ratios, tighter pitches, higher temperatures, and more demanding integration steps. “Dimensional shrinking in 2D is getting closer to its limits,” said Hichem M’Saad, CEO of ASM International. “So devices are moving into 3D. Once you go that direction, you get better performance by having new materials.” The result is an architectural shift that elevates materials engineering to the center of semiconductor progress. Gate dielectrics, etch-stop layers, liners, nucleation films, and encapsulation materials are no longer treated as passive unit processes. They influence device behavior, interconnect performance, and overall system characteristics. Achieving high performance increasingly requires deposition techniques capable of controlling matter one atomic layer at a time. Atomic-layer deposition Atomic-layer deposition (ALD) has become indispensable for managing these challenges, especially on the front end. ALD is not new, but its importance has surged as device dimensions approach scales where the number of atoms in a film becomes a limiting factor. High-k gate dielectrics, spacers, liners, nucleation layers, and work-function materials all benefit from ALD’s angstrom-level thickness control. BEOL interconnects also use ALD for diffusion barriers, caps, and etch-stop films, where aspect ratios exceed the reach of traditional PVD or PECVD. Unlike line-of-sight deposition, ALD’s sequential surface reactions let each atomic layer form uniformly, even in deep or narrow structures. This precision opens pathways to entirely new compounds and nanolaminates tailored for specific electrical, mechanical, or thermal properties. In practice, it enables foundries to create dielectric and barrier films that would be impossible to fabricate by any other means. “ALD is becoming necessary, especially for gate-all-around,” said Victor Moroz, fellow at Synopsys. “You build the structure one atom at a time and look at the surface reactions and how the next atom attaches. You try to make the chemistry such that the kink sites are more attractive, so you grow one monolayer at a time.” Uniformity is more than a convenience for these structures. It’s foundational. Even a small variation in ALD thickness can shift electrostatic control or introduce leakage pathways that accumulate across billions of transistors. “These structures are getting really complex,” said Joseph Ervin, managing director of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research. “The 3D geometries make it very challenging to make sure films are conformal. You can certainly go build and test it, but it takes a lot of iterations to get through. We use simulation to explore that space, such as how deposition occurs across the structure and how things diffuse on the surfaces to shorten the design cycle and get to a solution faster.” Fig. 1: Simulation of atomic layer deposition. Source: Lam Research “At the transistor level, conformality is essential,” added Moroz. “Between the adjacent channels, there’s about 10 or 11 nanometers of space, and you have to deposit the dielectric conformally from both sides. That takes about 2.5 nanometers on each side, so you only have 5 or 6 nanometers left for metal. You have to deposit this dielectric first and then the metal in that tiny space.” To achieve that level of precision, other deposition techniques are evolving as complementary solutions. “We can call it sputter epitaxial growth,” said Michael Schneider, vice president of semiconductors and precision optics for Von Ardenne. “During each revolution of the disk, you get a thickness increase of roughly one monolayer, or about 0.1 nanometers. This provides extremely precise control over the film’s thickness.” Sputter epitaxy doesn’t replace ALD for conformal structures, but it does provide an alternative for planar or symmetric layers that demand uniform stress and thickness control across large areas. It reflects how multiple thin-film approaches are now being tuned together to achieve atomic-level uniformity across different geometries. ALD surface chemistry ALD’s defining characteristic is its self-limiting surface chemistry. Films grow one monolayer at a time through alternating precursor pulses. Each pulse reacts with surface termination sites until they are fully consumed, allowing for extremely uniform deposition even in deep or narrow structures. “Moore’s Law right now is being driven more and more by new materials,” said M’Saad. “The best technique to deposit new material is ALD, because its self-limiting nature makes it possible to innovate and create new materials.” Fig. 2: ALD process flow. fetched_contents.text: PVD - The Cornerstone of Modern Semiconductor Manufacturing By Brian Bonar Deposition technology embodies the culmination of precision and innovation—qualities essential in today’s fast-evolving technological landscape. One such advanced technique is Physical Vapor Deposition (PVD), a sophisticated process that plays an indispensable role in crafting the ultra-thin films needed for semiconductor devices. While the nuances of PVD may be highly technical—even I’ll admit I’m not a technical expert—its importance as a cornerstone of modern semiconductor manufacturing cannot be overstated. Let’s explore why. Defining PVD In the realm of semiconductor manufacturing, precision and innovation are not just important; they’re non-negotiable. Physical Vapor Deposition, or PVD, is one of the foundational processes used to meet these demands. PVD is a vacuum-based technique in which a solid material, such as a metal or ceramic, is vaporized and deposited onto a substrate to form a thin film. This process enables the creation of layers with exceptional uniformity, purity, and adhesion. These characteristics are critical for semiconductor components such as transistors, diodes, and interconnects—the building blocks of high-performance microchips. Why is PVD Crucial to Semiconductors? Semiconductors are at the heart of virtually all modern technologies, from smartphones and electric vehicles to medical devices and AI systems. The performance of these devices depends heavily on the materials and processes used to manufacture them. Here is where PVD excels: 1. Precision: The PVD process ensures extremely thin and consistent layers, which are vital for the miniaturization of semiconductor devices. With technology nodes shrinking, the margin for error in layer thickness has become almost nonexistent. 2. Material Flexibility: PVD can work with a wide range of materials, enabling engineers to deposit metals, alloys, and compounds tailored to specific applications. This flexibility makes it suitable for diverse industries beyond semiconductors, including aerospace and optics. 3. Enhanced Performance: By producing films with high purity and adhesion, PVD contributes to the improved performance and longevity of semiconductor devices. These qualities ensure that devices can handle the increasing demands of today’s complex systems. Deposition Technology: Driving Innovation at Dalrada Dalrada Technology Group (Dalrada) specializes in providing cutting-edge solutions in thin-film deposition, including advanced PVD systems. Our technology delivers the precision, performance, and flexibility required for even the most challenging semiconductor applications. By partnering with clients, we enable them to push the boundaries of what’s possible—from creating faster microprocessors to enhancing energy efficiency in electronics. Dalrada’s deposition solutions support semiconductor companies across industries including aerospace, automotive, medical devices, computing, networking, and more. Other industrial appli- cations of ALD remained limited for 20 years, but during the past 10-15 years microelectronics has been the major driver for ALD technology. Branch report on which metals are deposited by which device class

In advanced-node semiconductor manufacturing, the evidence points to a clear hierarchy of deposition methods for metal films, with physical vapor deposition (PVD), chemical vapor deposition (CVD), and atomic layer deposition (ALD) being the most directly relevant classes for the question, while electron beam evaporation (EBE) and molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) appear to be more specialized or less central to metal-metal deposition in the provided evidence [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-R5][N5-F3].

## Which metals are deposited by PVD and their typical layer roles?
The evidence repeatedly positions PVD as the main method for metallic layers. It explicitly states that PVD deposits thin films of materials like aluminum, copper, titanium, gold, TiAl, NiCr, and silicon [N2-R1]. In semiconductor manufacturing context, PVD is described as the cornerstone technique for forming ultra-thin films with exceptional uniformity, purity, and adhesion, and it is especially relevant for interconnects, transistors, and diodes [N2-R2][N2-F2]. A separate source notes that PVD is used for “metal films” on both silicon and non-silicon substrates [N2-R3].

From the evidence, the metals deposited by PVD in advanced-node contexts include:
- **aluminum** [N2-R1][N2-F2]
- **copper** [N2-R1][N2-F2][N2-R5]
- **titanium** [N2-R1][N2-R4]
- **tungsten** [N2-R4][N3-R5]
- **titanium tungsten (TiW)** [N2-R4]
- **titanium aluminum (TiAl)** [N2-R1]
- **nickel chromium (NiCr)** [N2-R1]

The typical roles for PVD-deposited metals are:
- **interconnects**: PVD is described as central to creating the ultra-thin films needed for semiconductor interconnects [N2-F2].
- **barriers and adhesion layers**: Titanium and titanium tungsten are specifically noted as critical elements in PVD processing that attach subsequent structures to device elements [N2-R4].
- **multi-material stacks**: PVD can deposit alloys and compounds tailored to specific applications, including TiAl and NiCr [N2-R1][N2-R5].

## Which metals are deposited by CVD and their typical layer roles?
CVD is presented as complementary to PVD and especially relevant for conformal or more complex deposition scenarios. The evidence states that CVD is used for depositing high-quality films and that it bridges the gap between PVD and ALD by delivering excellent film quality [N7-R2][N7-R3]. A CVD-specific source notes that tungsten is used because of the extraordinarily good conformality of CVD from WF6, and that an adhesion/barrier layer such as Ti/TiN is necessary [N3-R5]. Another CVD-related source says that cobalt and cobalt silicide can be deposited in one chamber with tungsten in another [N3-R2].

From the evidence, the metals deposited by CVD in advanced-node contexts include:
- **tungsten** [N3-R5]
- **cobalt** [N3-R2]
- **cobalt silicide** [N3-R2]
- **tungsten silicide** [N3-R1]
- **tungsten nitride** [N5-F3]

The typical roles for CVD-deposited metals are:
- **interconnects and contacts**: Tungsten is highlighted for its conformality in CVD and for use in tungsten seed layers for tungsten CVD contact plug fill [N3-R5][N5-F3].
- **capping and barrier layers**: CVD is used where conformality and uniformity are needed, and tungsten nitride is explicitly noted as a material deposited by reaction of ammonia with tungsten [N5-F3].
- **diffusion-barrier-related materials**: CVD is used in tandem with barrier layers such as Ti/TiN, and in a patent example, cobalt silicide and metallic cobalt are deposited alongside tungsten [N3-R5][N3-R2].

## Which metals are deposited by EBE, ALD, or MBE and their typical layer roles?
The evidence for EBE is thinner than for PVD and CVD, but it is still present and indicates that EBE is used for thin-film deposition of metals. A source notes that titanium-aluminum alloy thin films can be deposited by electron beam evaporation, and another states that E-beam evaporation is used for aluminum into an atomized form for electronic materials and line substrates [N4-R2][N4-R5]. However, the provided evidence does not directly identify a broad set of advanced-node metals deposited exclusively by EBE in the same way it does for PVD and CVD.

For **ALD**, the evidence is much stronger. ALD is described as the most advanced deposition method in the market and as indispensable for managing challenges in advanced-node manufacturing, especially for ultra-thin films and conformal deposition [N1-R2][N1-R4]. It is explicitly tied to barrier films, diffusion barriers, caps, and etch-stop films in back-end-of-line (BEOL) interconnects [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that ALD is used for tantalum nitride (TaN) and that ALD TaN is a material of choice for certain semiconductor applications [N5-F3][N5-R5]. A patent example further indicates that ALD tantalum nitride is used to improve adhesion between copper structures and overlying materials [N5-R4].

For **MBE**, the evidence is more limited but still significant. MBE is described as a thin-film deposition technique used to grow high-quality crystalline thin films, and one source notes the growth of tantalum on semiconducting Ge substrates via MBE [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Another source describes MBE as a high-vacuum technique that allows growth of ultra-thin layers with unmatched accuracy and uniformity [N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not clearly identify a broad set of advanced-node metals deposited by MBE in the same way it does for PVD and CVD.

So, from the provided evidence, the metals deposited by EBE, ALD, or MBE in advanced-node contexts are:
- **EBE**: aluminum, titanium-aluminum alloy, and possibly other metals used in thin-film applications [N4-R2][N4-R5]
- **ALD**: tantalum nitride (TaN), and more broadly barrier films, caps, and etch-stop films [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R5]
- **MBE**: tantalum and other high-quality crystalline thin films [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]

## Bottom line
The evidence supports the following picture for advanced-node metal deposition:
- **PVD** is the most broadly used method for metallic layers, including aluminum, copper, titanium, tungsten, TiW, TiAl, NiCr, and others [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5].
- **CVD** is used for conformal and barrier-related layers, especially tungsten, cobalt, cobalt silicide, and tungsten silicide, often in combination with adhesion/barrier layers [N3-R5][N3-R2][N3-R1].
- **ALD** is reserved for ultra-thin, conformal, and barrier-like layers, especially tantalum nitride and other nanolaminates that are difficult to make with traditional methods [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R5].
- **EBE** appears to be used for thin-film metals such as aluminum and titanium-aluminum alloy, but its role is more specialized in the evidence provided [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- **MBE** is used for high-quality crystalline thin films, including tantalum on semiconducting substrates, but the evidence is more limited and not as central to the general metal-metal deposition picture [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a layered use pattern: PVD for metallic interconnects and barriers, CVD for conformal contacts and diffusion-barrier-related materials, and ALD for ultra-thin, highly conformal barrier and cap layers [N1-R4][N1-F1][N5-F3].

## Integrated final answer: which devices are used, which metals they deposit, and why

In advanced-node chip manufacturing, the metal-film deposition process is not a one-size-fits-all recipe. Instead, it is a carefully selected combination of deposition methods tailored to the metal, layer role, geometry, and process step. Based on the provided branch reports, the most relevant methods in advanced-node metal-layer processing are:

- **physical vapor deposition (PVD)**
- **chemical vapor deposition (CVD)**
- **atomic layer deposition (ALD)**
- **electron beam evaporation (EBE)**
- **molecular beam epitaxy (MBE)**

The evidence also suggests that **MBE** is more specialized and less central to general metal-metal deposition in the provided sources, while **EBE** is present but thinner in the evidence than PVD and CVD [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-R5][N5-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 1) Which devices are actually used in advanced-node chip manufacturing?

### Commonly used methods
The branch reports indicate that **PVD, CVD, and ALD** are the most commonly used in advanced-node metal-layer processing [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1].

- **PVD** is described as the cornerstone technique for semiconductor manufacturing and especially relevant for metallic layers [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is presented as complementary to PVD and useful where conformality and film quality matter [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].
- **ALD** is described as the most advanced deposition method in the market and indispensable for managing advanced-node challenges, especially for ultra-thin, conformal films [N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1].

### Methods reserved for specific layers or features only
The evidence suggests that certain methods are used for specific layers or features rather than broadly for all metals:

- **ALD** is reserved for ultra-thin, conformal barrier films, caps, and etch-stop films in BEOL interconnects, where traditional PVD or PECVD may not reach [N1-F1].
- **CVD** is used for conformal contacts and for tungsten seed layers, while ALD is used for tantalum nitride and other barrier-like nanolaminates [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **EBE** appears to be used more selectively for thin-film metals such as aluminum and titanium-aluminum alloy, but the evidence is thinner and less central than for PVD and CVD [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### How device availability has changed with node scaling
The evidence reflects a clear trend: as nodes scale into sub-10nm and below, the need for **atomic-level uniformity, conformality, and nanoscale control** has increased, making **ALD** increasingly necessary for gate-all-around and other 3D structures [N1-R4][N1-F1][N1-R5]. At the same time, **PVD** remains ideal for metallic layers and planar or symmetric layers that require uniform stress and thickness control, while **CVD** bridges the gap between PVD and ALD by delivering excellent film quality and conformality for contacts and barrier-related materials [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].

So, the device availability picture is:
- **PVD** continues to be central and widely used for metallic layers.
- **CVD** becomes more important for conformal contacts and barrier-related materials.
- **ALD** becomes increasingly essential for the smallest geometries and most challenging barrier and cap layers.
- **EBE** and **MBE** are present but more specialized or limited in the provided evidence [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 2) Which metals are deposited by which device class?

### PVD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
The evidence identifies a broad set of metals deposited by PVD in semiconductor manufacturing:

- **aluminum**
- **copper**
- **titanium**
- **tungsten**
- **titanium tungsten (TiW)**
- **titanium aluminum (TiAl)**
- **nickel chromium (NiCr)**
- **silicon** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]

PVD is especially relevant for:
- **interconnects** [N2-F2]
- **barriers and adhesion layers** [N2-R4]
- **multi-material stacks** and alloys [N2-R1][N2-R5]

### CVD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
CVD is used for conformal and barrier-related deposition, with the evidence identifying:

- **tungsten**
- **cobalt**
- **cobalt silicide**
- **tungsten silicide**
- **tungsten nitride**
- **tantalum nitride** [N3-R5][N3-R2][N3-R1][N5-F3]

CVD is especially used for:
- **interconnects and contacts** [N3-R5]
- **capping and barrier layers** [N3-R5][N5-F3]
- **diffusion-barrier-related materials** [N3-R5][N3-R2]

### EBE-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
The evidence is thinner, but it does indicate that EBE is used for thin-film metals such as:

- **aluminum**
- **titanium-aluminum alloy**

It is also used for **atomized aluminum** in electronic materials and line substrates [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### ALD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
ALD is the clearest example of a method reserved for ultra-thin, conformal layers. The evidence identifies:

- **tantalum nitride (TaN)** [N5-F3][N5-R5]
- **tungsten nitride**
- **barrier films**
- **caps**
- **etch-stop films**
- **nanolaminates and ultra-thin films** [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R5]

### MBE-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
MBE is described as a high-quality crystalline thin-film technique, with evidence that it is used for:

- **tantalum** on semiconducting substrates
- **high-quality crystalline thin films** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]

The evidence is more limited than for PVD and CVD, so MBE appears to be more specialized than general-purpose.

---

## 3) Why each device is chosen for its metal

### Why a device is selected for purity, thickness, or uniformity needs
The evidence shows that the choice of deposition method is driven by the film’s required properties:

- **PVD** is selected because it produces **high-purity films** in a vacuum environment, which minimizes contamination [N7-R4]. This makes it ideal for metallic layers where purity matters, such as interconnects and adhesion layers [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is selected because it can deliver **excellent film quality** and is useful for conformal layers, especially in contacts and barrier-related structures [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].
- **ALD** is selected because it offers **angstrom-level thickness control** and can deposit **ultra-thin, conformal films** even in deep or narrow structures [N1-R4][N1-F1]. This is especially important for advanced-node barrier and cap layers.
- **EBE** is selected for thin-film applications such as **aluminum** and **titanium-aluminum alloy**, where atomization and thin-film quality matter [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Why a device is selected for adhesion or interface requirements
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes interface and adhesion requirements:

- **Titanium and titanium tungsten (Ti/TiW)** are specifically noted as critical elements in PVD processing that attach subsequent structures to device elements [N2-R4]. This means PVD is chosen when a good **adhesion layer** is needed.
- **CVD** is often used with an **adhesion/barrier layer** such as Ti/TiN, which improves the interface for subsequent deposition [N3-R5].
- **ALD tantalum nitride (TaN)** is used to improve adhesion between an underlying copper structure and overlying materials [N5-R4].
- **ALD** is chosen because its self-limiting surface chemistry allows films to grow one monolayer at a time, improving **interface uniformity** and **film continuity** in complex geometries [N1-F1].

### Why a device is selected for compatibility with advanced-node process steps
The evidence shows that the choice is also driven by the broader process flow:

- **PVD** is used when **metallic layers** and **planar or symmetric layers** are needed, and it is central to interconnect fabrication [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is used when **conformal contacts** or **barrier-related materials** are needed, especially in conjunction with adhesion layers [N3-R5].
- **ALD** is used when **nanoscale control**, **3D geometries**, and **ultra-thin conformal films** are required, making it indispensable for advanced-node BEOL processing [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **EBE** is used in thin-film applications where atomization and thin-film quality matter, though it appears more specialized [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- **MBE** is used for **high-quality crystalline thin films**, including tantalum on semiconducting substrates, where crystal quality matters more than general metal-metal deposition [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 4) Advanced-node metal layer roles and deposition-method fit

### Which metal layers are used in interconnects, barriers, capping, or diffusion layers?
The evidence identifies several key roles:

- **Interconnects**: PVD is used for metallic interconnects [N2-F2]. CVD is used for tungsten seed layers and contacts [N3-R5]. ALD is used for diffusion barriers, caps, and etch-stop films in BEOL [N1-F1].
- **Barriers**: PVD provides titanium and titanium tungsten as adhesion/barrier layers [N2-R4]. CVD is used alongside barrier layers such as Ti/TiN [N3-R5]. ALD tantalum nitride improves adhesion between copper structures and overlying materials [N5-R4].
- **Capping and etch-stop**: ALD is used for caps and etch-stop films where conformality is critical [N1-F1].
- **Diffusion barriers**: CVD and ALD are both used for diffusion barriers, including tungsten nitride and tantalum nitride [N3-R5][N5-F3].

### How geometry and thickness requirements shape the choice of deposition method
The evidence clearly shows that geometry and thickness are central to method selection:

- **PVD** is good for metallic layers but relatively poor in step coverage for deep trenches or high-aspect-ratio structures [N7-R1].
- **CVD** is better for conformal layers, especially tungsten in contacts and for barrier-related materials [N3-R5][N7-R2].
- **ALD** is the best fit for **ultra-thin**, **conformal**, and **deep/narrow structures**, because its sequential surface reactions allow uniform deposition even in difficult geometries [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **EBE** is used where thin-film quality matters, but it is not as central to the general picture as PVD and CVD [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### How the same layer may use multiple methods in different process steps
The evidence supports the idea that a single layer can involve multiple methods in different steps. For example:

- **CVD** may be used for a **seed layer or contact fill**, while **ALD** is used for a **barrier or cap layer** [N3-R5][N1-F1].
- **PVD** may be used for the **base metallic layer**, while **CVD** or **ALD** is used for the **adhesion/barrier or diffusion barrier** [N2-R4][N3-R5][N5-R4].

This hybrid approach reflects the need to balance **purity, conformality, adhesion, and process compatibility** across the same layer.

---

## 5) Bottom line

In advanced-node chip manufacturing, the metal-film deposition landscape is shaped by the following:

| Device        | Metals typically deposited           | Layer roles and why it is chosen                                                                 | Best fit for geometry/thickness                          |
|---------------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| **PVD**       | Al, Cu, Ti, W, TiW, TiAl, NiCr     | Interconnects, adhesion/barriers, multi-material stacks; high purity and uniformity [N2-R1][N2-F2] | Planar or symmetric layers; metallic interconnects [N2-R4] |
| **CVD**       | W, Co, CoSi, WSi, WxNy, TaNx       | Contacts, barrier-related materials, conformal films [N3-R5][N5-F3]                               | Conformal contacts and barrier-related layers [N3-R5]     |
| **ALD**       | TaNx, WxNy, barrier/cap/etch-stop  | Ultra-thin, conformal barrier, cap, and etch-stop films [N1-F1][N5-F3]                           | Deep/narrow structures, nanoscale control [N1-F1]         |
| **EBE**       | Al, TiAl alloy                     | Thin-film metals in specialized applications [N4-R2][N4-R5]                                      | More specialized than PVD/CVD; atomized thin films [N4-R5] |
| **MBE**       | Ta, crystalline thin films          | High-quality crystalline thin films [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]                                        | More specialized; not central to general metal-metal deposition [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5] |

## Final conclusion
In today’s advanced-node chip manufacturing, **PVD, CVD, and ALD** are the most important methods for metal-film deposition, while **EBE** and **MBE** are present but more specialized or limited in scope. The choice of method depends on the metal, the layer role, the geometry, and the need for purity, uniformity, adhesion, and compatibility with the overall process. The evidence supports a layered approach: **PVD** for metallic interconnects and barriers, **CVD** for conformal contacts and barrier-related materials, and **ALD** for ultra-thin, conformal barrier and cap layers in the most advanced geometries [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-F2][N3-R5][N5-F3][N1-F1].

Branch report on which metals are deposited by which device class

In advanced-node semiconductor manufacturing, the evidence points to a clear hierarchy of deposition methods for metal films, with physical vapor deposition (PVD), chemical vapor deposition (CVD), and atomic layer deposition (ALD) being the most directly relevant classes for the question, while electron beam evaporation (EBE) and molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) appear to be more specialized or less central to metal-metal deposition in the provided evidence [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-R5][N5-F3].

## Which metals are deposited by PVD and their typical layer roles?
The evidence repeatedly positions PVD as the main method for metallic layers. It explicitly states that PVD deposits thin films of materials like aluminum, copper, titanium, gold, TiAl, NiCr, and silicon [N2-R1]. In semiconductor manufacturing context, PVD is described as the cornerstone technique for forming ultra-thin films with exceptional uniformity, purity, and adhesion, and it is especially relevant for interconnects, transistors, and diodes [N2-R2][N2-F2]. A separate source notes that PVD is used for “metal films” on both silicon and non-silicon substrates [N2-R3].

From the evidence, the metals deposited by PVD in advanced-node contexts include:
- **aluminum** [N2-R1][N2-F2]
- **copper** [N2-R1][N2-F2][N2-R5]
- **titanium** [N2-R1][N2-R4]
- **tungsten** [N2-R4][N3-R5]
- **titanium tungsten (TiW)** [N2-R4]
- **titanium aluminum (TiAl)** [N2-R1]
- **nickel chromium (NiCr)** [N2-R1]

The typical roles for PVD-deposited metals are:
- **interconnects**: PVD is described as central to creating the ultra-thin films needed for semiconductor interconnects [N2-F2].
- **barriers and adhesion layers**: Titanium and titanium tungsten are specifically noted as critical elements in PVD processing that attach subsequent structures to device elements [N2-R4].
- **multi-material stacks**: PVD can deposit alloys and compounds tailored to specific applications, including TiAl and NiCr [N2-R1][N2-R5].

## Which metals are deposited by CVD and their typical layer roles?
CVD is presented as complementary to PVD and especially relevant for conformal or more complex deposition scenarios. The evidence states that CVD is used for depositing high-quality films and that it bridges the gap between PVD and ALD by delivering excellent film quality [N7-R2][N7-R3]. A CVD-specific source notes that tungsten is used because of the extraordinarily good conformality of CVD from WF6, and that an adhesion/barrier layer such as Ti/TiN is necessary [N3-R5]. Another CVD-related source says that cobalt and cobalt silicide can be deposited in one chamber with tungsten in another [N3-R2].

From the evidence, the metals deposited by CVD in advanced-node contexts include:
- **tungsten** [N3-R5]
- **cobalt** [N3-R2]
- **cobalt silicide** [N3-R2]
- **tungsten silicide** [N3-R1]
- **tungsten nitride** [N5-F3]

The typical roles for CVD-deposited metals are:
- **interconnects and contacts**: Tungsten is highlighted for its conformality in CVD and for use in tungsten seed layers for tungsten CVD contact plug fill [N3-R5][N5-F3].
- **capping and barrier layers**: CVD is used where conformality and uniformity are needed, and tungsten nitride is explicitly noted as a material deposited by reaction of ammonia with tungsten [N5-F3].
- **diffusion-barrier-related materials**: CVD is used in tandem with barrier layers such as Ti/TiN, and in a patent example, cobalt silicide and metallic cobalt are deposited alongside tungsten [N3-R5][N3-R2].

## Which metals are deposited by EBE, ALD, or MBE and their typical layer roles?
The evidence for EBE is thinner than for PVD and CVD, but it is still present and indicates that EBE is used for thin-film deposition of metals. A source notes that titanium-aluminum alloy thin films can be deposited by electron beam evaporation, and another states that E-beam evaporation is used for aluminum into an atomized form for electronic materials and line substrates [N4-R2][N4-R5]. However, the provided evidence does not directly identify a broad set of advanced-node metals deposited exclusively by EBE in the same way it does for PVD and CVD.

For **ALD**, the evidence is much stronger. ALD is described as the most advanced deposition method in the market and as indispensable for managing challenges in advanced-node manufacturing, especially for ultra-thin films and conformal deposition [N1-R2][N1-R4]. It is explicitly tied to barrier films, diffusion barriers, caps, and etch-stop films in back-end-of-line (BEOL) interconnects [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that ALD is used for tantalum nitride (TaN) and that ALD TaN is a material of choice for certain semiconductor applications [N5-F3][N5-R5]. A patent example further indicates that ALD tantalum nitride is used to improve adhesion between copper structures and overlying materials [N5-R4].

For **MBE**, the evidence is more limited but still significant. MBE is described as a thin-film deposition technique used to grow high-quality crystalline thin films, and one source notes the growth of tantalum on semiconducting Ge substrates via MBE [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Another source describes MBE as a high-vacuum technique that allows growth of ultra-thin layers with unmatched accuracy and uniformity [N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not clearly identify a broad set of advanced-node metals deposited by MBE in the same way it does for PVD and CVD.

So, from the provided evidence, the metals deposited by EBE, ALD, or MBE in advanced-node contexts are:
- **EBE**: aluminum, titanium-aluminum alloy, and possibly other metals used in thin-film applications [N4-R2][N4-R5]
- **ALD**: tantalum nitride (TaN), and more broadly barrier films, caps, and etch-stop films [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R5]
- **MBE**: tantalum and other high-quality crystalline thin films [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]

## Bottom line
The evidence supports the following picture for advanced-node metal deposition:
- **PVD** is the most broadly used method for metallic layers, including aluminum, copper, titanium, tungsten, TiW, TiAl, NiCr, and others [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5].
- **CVD** is used for conformal and barrier-related layers, especially tungsten, cobalt, cobalt silicide, and tungsten silicide, often in combination with adhesion/barrier layers [N3-R5][N3-R2][N3-R1].
- **ALD** is reserved for ultra-thin, conformal, and barrier-like layers, especially tantalum nitride and other nanolaminates that are difficult to make with traditional methods [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R5].
- **EBE** appears to be used for thin-film metals such as aluminum and titanium-aluminum alloy, but its role is more specialized in the evidence provided [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- **MBE** is used for high-quality crystalline thin films, including tantalum on semiconducting substrates, but the evidence is more limited and not as central to the general metal-metal deposition picture [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a layered use pattern: PVD for metallic interconnects and barriers, CVD for conformal contacts and diffusion-barrier-related materials, and ALD for ultra-thin, highly conformal barrier and cap layers [N1-R4][N1-F1][N5-F3].

## Integrated final answer: which devices are used, which metals they deposit, and why

In advanced-node chip manufacturing, the metal-film deposition process is not a one-size-fits-all recipe. Instead, it is a carefully selected combination of deposition methods tailored to the metal, layer role, geometry, and process step. Based on the provided branch reports, the most relevant methods in advanced-node metal-layer processing are:

- **physical vapor deposition (PVD)**
- **chemical vapor deposition (CVD)**
- **atomic layer deposition (ALD)**
- **electron beam evaporation (EBE)**
- **molecular beam epitaxy (MBE)**

The evidence also suggests that **MBE** is more specialized and less central to general metal-metal deposition in the provided sources, while **EBE** is present but thinner in the evidence than PVD and CVD [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-R5][N5-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 1) Which devices are actually used in advanced-node chip manufacturing?

### Commonly used methods
The branch reports indicate that **PVD, CVD, and ALD** are the most commonly used in advanced-node metal-layer processing [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1].

- **PVD** is described as the cornerstone technique for semiconductor manufacturing and especially relevant for metallic layers [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is presented as complementary to PVD and useful where conformality and film quality matter [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].
- **ALD** is described as the most advanced deposition method in the market and indispensable for managing advanced-node challenges, especially for ultra-thin, conformal films [N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1].

### Methods reserved for specific layers or features only
The evidence suggests that certain methods are used for specific layers or features rather than broadly for all metals:

- **ALD** is reserved for ultra-thin, conformal barrier films, caps, and etch-stop films in BEOL interconnects, where traditional PVD or PECVD may not reach [N1-F1].
- **CVD** is used for conformal contacts and for tungsten seed layers, while ALD is used for tantalum nitride and other barrier-like nanolaminates [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **EBE** appears to be used more selectively for thin-film metals such as aluminum and titanium-aluminum alloy, but the evidence is thinner and less central than for PVD and CVD [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### How device availability has changed with node scaling
The evidence reflects a clear trend: as nodes scale into sub-10nm and below, the need for **atomic-level uniformity, conformality, and nanoscale control** has increased, making **ALD** increasingly necessary for gate-all-around and other 3D structures [N1-R4][N1-F1][N1-R5]. At the same time, **PVD** remains ideal for metallic layers and planar or symmetric layers that require uniform stress and thickness control, while **CVD** bridges the gap between PVD and ALD by delivering excellent film quality and conformality for contacts and barrier-related materials [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].

So, the device availability picture is:
- **PVD** continues to be central and widely used for metallic layers.
- **CVD** becomes more important for conformal contacts and barrier-related materials.
- **ALD** becomes increasingly essential for the smallest geometries and most challenging barrier and cap layers.
- **EBE** and **MBE** are present but more specialized or limited in the provided evidence [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 2) Which metals are deposited by which device class?

### PVD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
The evidence identifies a broad set of metals deposited by PVD in semiconductor manufacturing:

- **aluminum**
- **copper**
- **titanium**
- **tungsten**
- **titanium tungsten (TiW)**
- **titanium aluminum (TiAl)**
- **nickel chromium (NiCr)**
- **silicon** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]

PVD is especially relevant for:
- **interconnects** [N2-F2]
- **barriers and adhesion layers** [N2-R4]
- **multi-material stacks** and alloys [N2-R1][N2-R5]

### CVD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
CVD is used for conformal and barrier-related deposition, with the evidence identifying:

- **tungsten**
- **cobalt**
- **cobalt silicide**
- **tungsten silicide**
- **tungsten nitride**
- **tantalum nitride** [N3-R5][N3-R2][N3-R1][N5-F3]

CVD is especially used for:
- **interconnects and contacts** [N3-R5]
- **capping and barrier layers** [N3-R5][N5-F3]
- **diffusion-barrier-related materials** [N3-R5][N3-R2]

### EBE-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
The evidence is thinner, but it does indicate that EBE is used for thin-film metals such as:

- **aluminum**
- **titanium-aluminum alloy**

It is also used for **atomized aluminum** in electronic materials and line substrates [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### ALD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
ALD is the clearest example of a method reserved for ultra-thin, conformal layers. The evidence identifies:

- **tantalum nitride (TaN)** [N5-F3][N5-R5]
- **tungsten nitride**
- **barrier films**
- **caps**
- **etch-stop films**
- **nanolaminates and ultra-thin films** [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R5]

### MBE-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
MBE is described as a high-quality crystalline thin-film technique, with evidence that it is used for:

- **tantalum** on semiconducting substrates
- **high-quality crystalline thin films** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]

The evidence is more limited than for PVD and CVD, so MBE appears to be more specialized than general-purpose.

---

## 3) Why each device is chosen for its metal

### Why a device is selected for purity, thickness, or uniformity needs
The evidence shows that the choice of deposition method is driven by the film’s required properties:

- **PVD** is selected because it produces **high-purity films** in a vacuum environment, which minimizes contamination [N7-R4]. This makes it ideal for metallic layers where purity matters, such as interconnects and adhesion layers [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is selected because it can deliver **excellent film quality** and is useful for conformal layers, especially in contacts and barrier-related structures [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].
- **ALD** is selected because it offers **angstrom-level thickness control** and can deposit **ultra-thin, conformal films** even in deep or narrow structures [N1-R4][N1-F1]. This is especially important for advanced-node barrier and cap layers.
- **EBE** is selected for thin-film applications such as **aluminum** and **titanium-aluminum alloy**, where atomization and thin-film quality matter [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Why a device is selected for adhesion or interface requirements
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes interface and adhesion requirements:

- **Titanium and titanium tungsten (Ti/TiW)** are specifically noted as critical elements in PVD processing that attach subsequent structures to device elements [N2-R4]. This means PVD is chosen when a good **adhesion layer** is needed.
- **CVD** is often used with an **adhesion/barrier layer** such as Ti/TiN, which improves the interface for subsequent deposition [N3-R5].
- **ALD tantalum nitride (TaN)** is used to improve adhesion between an underlying copper structure and overlying materials [N5-R4].
- **ALD** is chosen because its self-limiting surface chemistry allows films to grow one monolayer at a time, improving **interface uniformity** and **film continuity** in complex geometries [N1-F1].

### Why a device is selected for compatibility with advanced-node process steps
The evidence shows that the choice is also driven by the broader process flow:

- **PVD** is used when **metallic layers** and **planar or symmetric layers** are needed, and it is central to interconnect fabrication [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is used when **conformal contacts** or **barrier-related materials** are needed, especially in conjunction with adhesion layers [N3-R5].
- **ALD** is used when **nanoscale control**, **3D geometries**, and **ultra-thin conformal films** are required, making it indispensable for advanced-node BEOL processing [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **EBE** is used in thin-film applications where atomization and thin-film quality matter, though it appears more specialized [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- **MBE** is used for **high-quality crystalline thin films**, including tantalum on semiconducting substrates, where crystal quality matters more than general metal-metal deposition [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 4) Advanced-node metal layer roles and deposition-method fit

### Which metal layers are used in interconnects, barriers, capping, or diffusion layers?
The evidence identifies several key roles:

- **Interconnects**: PVD is used for metallic interconnects [N2-F2]. CVD is used for tungsten seed layers and contacts [N3-R5]. ALD is used for diffusion barriers, caps, and etch-stop films in BEOL [N1-F1].
- **Barriers**: PVD provides titanium and titanium tungsten as adhesion/barrier layers [N2-R4]. CVD is used alongside barrier layers such as Ti/TiN [N3-R5]. ALD tantalum nitride improves adhesion between copper structures and overlying materials [N5-R4].
- **Capping and etch-stop**: ALD is used for caps and etch-stop films where conformality is critical [N1-F1].
- **Diffusion barriers**: CVD and ALD are both used for diffusion barriers, including tungsten nitride and tantalum nitride [N3-R5][N5-F3].

### How geometry and thickness requirements shape the choice of deposition method
The evidence clearly shows that geometry and thickness are central to method selection:

- **PVD** is good for metallic layers but relatively poor in step coverage for deep trenches or high-aspect-ratio structures [N7-R1].
- **CVD** is better for conformal layers, especially tungsten in contacts and for barrier-related materials [N3-R5][N7-R2].
- **ALD** is the best fit for **ultra-thin**, **conformal**, and **deep/narrow structures**, because its sequential surface reactions allow uniform deposition even in difficult geometries [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **EBE** is used where thin-film quality matters, but it is not as central to the general picture as PVD and CVD [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### How the same layer may use multiple methods in different process steps
The evidence supports the idea that a single layer can involve multiple methods in different steps. For example:

- **CVD** may be used for a **seed layer or contact fill**, while **ALD** is used for a **barrier or cap layer** [N3-R5][N1-F1].
- **PVD** may be used for the **base metallic layer**, while **CVD** or **ALD** is used for the **adhesion/barrier or diffusion barrier** [N2-R4][N3-R5][N5-R4].

This hybrid approach reflects the need to balance **purity, conformality, adhesion, and process compatibility** across the same layer.

---

## 5) Bottom line

In advanced-node chip manufacturing, the metal-film deposition landscape is shaped by the following:

| Device        | Metals typically deposited           | Layer roles and why it is chosen                                                                 | Best fit for geometry/thickness                          |
|---------------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| **PVD**       | Al, Cu, Ti, W, TiW, TiAl, NiCr     | Interconnects, adhesion/barriers, multi-material stacks; high purity and uniformity [N2-R1][N2-F2] | Planar or symmetric layers; metallic interconnects [N2-R4] |
| **CVD**       | W, Co, CoSi, WSi, WxNy, TaNx       | Contacts, barrier-related materials, conformal films [N3-R5][N5-F3]                               | Conformal contacts and barrier-related layers [N3-R5]     |
| **ALD**       | TaNx, WxNy, barrier/cap/etch-stop  | Ultra-thin, conformal barrier, cap, and etch-stop films [N1-F1][N5-F3]                           | Deep/narrow structures, nanoscale control [N1-F1]         |
| **EBE**       | Al, TiAl alloy                     | Thin-film metals in specialized applications [N4-R2][N4-R5]                                      | More specialized than PVD/CVD; atomized thin films [N4-R5] |
| **MBE**       | Ta, crystalline thin films          | High-quality crystalline thin films [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]                                        | More specialized; not central to general metal-metal deposition [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5] |

## Final conclusion
In today’s advanced-node chip manufacturing, **PVD, CVD, and ALD** are the most important methods for metal-film deposition, while **EBE** and **MBE** are present but more specialized or limited in scope. The choice of method depends on the metal, the layer role, the geometry, and the need for purity, uniformity, adhesion, and compatibility with the overall process. The evidence supports a layered approach: **PVD** for metallic interconnects and barriers, **CVD** for conformal contacts and barrier-related materials, and **ALD** for ultra-thin, conformal barrier and cap layers in the most advanced geometries [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-F2][N3-R5][N5-F3][N1-F1].

Branch report on which metals are deposited by which device class

In advanced-node semiconductor manufacturing, the evidence points to a clear hierarchy of deposition methods for metal films, with physical vapor deposition (PVD), chemical vapor deposition (CVD), and atomic layer deposition (ALD) being the most directly relevant classes for the question, while electron beam evaporation (EBE) and molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) appear to be more specialized or less central to metal-metal deposition in the provided evidence [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-R5][N5-F3].

## Which metals are deposited by PVD and their typical layer roles?
The evidence repeatedly positions PVD as the main method for metallic layers. It explicitly states that PVD deposits thin films of materials like aluminum, copper, titanium, gold, TiAl, NiCr, and silicon [N2-R1]. In semiconductor manufacturing context, PVD is described as the cornerstone technique for forming ultra-thin films with exceptional uniformity, purity, and adhesion, and it is especially relevant for interconnects, transistors, and diodes [N2-R2][N2-F2]. A separate source notes that PVD is used for “metal films” on both silicon and non-silicon substrates [N2-R3].

From the evidence, the metals deposited by PVD in advanced-node contexts include:
- **aluminum** [N2-R1][N2-F2]
- **copper** [N2-R1][N2-F2][N2-R5]
- **titanium** [N2-R1][N2-R4]
- **tungsten** [N2-R4][N3-R5]
- **titanium tungsten (TiW)** [N2-R4]
- **titanium aluminum (TiAl)** [N2-R1]
- **nickel chromium (NiCr)** [N2-R1]

The typical roles for PVD-deposited metals are:
- **interconnects**: PVD is described as central to creating the ultra-thin films needed for semiconductor interconnects [N2-F2].
- **barriers and adhesion layers**: Titanium and titanium tungsten are specifically noted as critical elements in PVD processing that attach subsequent structures to device elements [N2-R4].
- **multi-material stacks**: PVD can deposit alloys and compounds tailored to specific applications, including TiAl and NiCr [N2-R1][N2-R5].

## Which metals are deposited by CVD and their typical layer roles?
CVD is presented as complementary to PVD and especially relevant for conformal or more complex deposition scenarios. The evidence states that CVD is used for depositing high-quality films and that it bridges the gap between PVD and ALD by delivering excellent film quality [N7-R2][N7-R3]. A CVD-specific source notes that tungsten is used because of the extraordinarily good conformality of CVD from WF6, and that an adhesion/barrier layer such as Ti/TiN is necessary [N3-R5]. Another CVD-related source says that cobalt and cobalt silicide can be deposited in one chamber with tungsten in another [N3-R2].

From the evidence, the metals deposited by CVD in advanced-node contexts include:
- **tungsten** [N3-R5]
- **cobalt** [N3-R2]
- **cobalt silicide** [N3-R2]
- **tungsten silicide** [N3-R1]
- **tungsten nitride** [N5-F3]

The typical roles for CVD-deposited metals are:
- **interconnects and contacts**: Tungsten is highlighted for its conformality in CVD and for use in tungsten seed layers for tungsten CVD contact plug fill [N3-R5][N5-F3].
- **capping and barrier layers**: CVD is used where conformality and uniformity are needed, and tungsten nitride is explicitly noted as a material deposited by reaction of ammonia with tungsten [N5-F3].
- **diffusion-barrier-related materials**: CVD is used in tandem with barrier layers such as Ti/TiN, and in a patent example, cobalt silicide and metallic cobalt are deposited alongside tungsten [N3-R5][N3-R2].

## Which metals are deposited by EBE, ALD, or MBE and their typical layer roles?
The evidence for EBE is thinner than for PVD and CVD, but it is still present and indicates that EBE is used for thin-film deposition of metals. A source notes that titanium-aluminum alloy thin films can be deposited by electron beam evaporation, and another states that E-beam evaporation is used for aluminum into an atomized form for electronic materials and line substrates [N4-R2][N4-R5]. However, the provided evidence does not directly identify a broad set of advanced-node metals deposited exclusively by EBE in the same way it does for PVD and CVD.

For **ALD**, the evidence is much stronger. ALD is described as the most advanced deposition method in the market and as indispensable for managing challenges in advanced-node manufacturing, especially for ultra-thin films and conformal deposition [N1-R2][N1-R4]. It is explicitly tied to barrier films, diffusion barriers, caps, and etch-stop films in back-end-of-line (BEOL) interconnects [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that ALD is used for tantalum nitride (TaN) and that ALD TaN is a material of choice for certain semiconductor applications [N5-F3][N5-R5]. A patent example further indicates that ALD tantalum nitride is used to improve adhesion between copper structures and overlying materials [N5-R4].

For **MBE**, the evidence is more limited but still significant. MBE is described as a thin-film deposition technique used to grow high-quality crystalline thin films, and one source notes the growth of tantalum on semiconducting Ge substrates via MBE [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Another source describes MBE as a high-vacuum technique that allows growth of ultra-thin layers with unmatched accuracy and uniformity [N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not clearly identify a broad set of advanced-node metals deposited by MBE in the same way it does for PVD and CVD.

So, from the provided evidence, the metals deposited by EBE, ALD, or MBE in advanced-node contexts are:
- **EBE**: aluminum, titanium-aluminum alloy, and possibly other metals used in thin-film applications [N4-R2][N4-R5]
- **ALD**: tantalum nitride (TaN), and more broadly barrier films, caps, and etch-stop films [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R5]
- **MBE**: tantalum and other high-quality crystalline thin films [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]

## Bottom line
The evidence supports the following picture for advanced-node metal deposition:
- **PVD** is the most broadly used method for metallic layers, including aluminum, copper, titanium, tungsten, TiW, TiAl, NiCr, and others [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5].
- **CVD** is used for conformal and barrier-related layers, especially tungsten, cobalt, cobalt silicide, and tungsten silicide, often in combination with adhesion/barrier layers [N3-R5][N3-R2][N3-R1].
- **ALD** is reserved for ultra-thin, conformal, and barrier-like layers, especially tantalum nitride and other nanolaminates that are difficult to make with traditional methods [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R5].
- **EBE** appears to be used for thin-film metals such as aluminum and titanium-aluminum alloy, but its role is more specialized in the evidence provided [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- **MBE** is used for high-quality crystalline thin films, including tantalum on semiconducting substrates, but the evidence is more limited and not as central to the general metal-metal deposition picture [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a layered use pattern: PVD for metallic interconnects and barriers, CVD for conformal contacts and diffusion-barrier-related materials, and ALD for ultra-thin, highly conformal barrier and cap layers [N1-R4][N1-F1][N5-F3].

## Integrated final answer: which devices are used, which metals they deposit, and why

In advanced-node chip manufacturing, the metal-film deposition process is not a one-size-fits-all recipe. Instead, it is a carefully selected combination of deposition methods tailored to the metal, layer role, geometry, and process step. Based on the provided branch reports, the most relevant methods in advanced-node metal-layer processing are:

- **physical vapor deposition (PVD)**
- **chemical vapor deposition (CVD)**
- **atomic layer deposition (ALD)**
- **electron beam evaporation (EBE)**
- **molecular beam epitaxy (MBE)**

The evidence also suggests that **MBE** is more specialized and less central to general metal-metal deposition in the provided sources, while **EBE** is present but thinner in the evidence than PVD and CVD [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-R5][N5-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 1) Which devices are actually used in advanced-node chip manufacturing?

### Commonly used methods
The branch reports indicate that **PVD, CVD, and ALD** are the most commonly used in advanced-node metal-layer processing [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1].

- **PVD** is described as the cornerstone technique for semiconductor manufacturing and especially relevant for metallic layers [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is presented as complementary to PVD and useful where conformality and film quality matter [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].
- **ALD** is described as the most advanced deposition method in the market and indispensable for managing advanced-node challenges, especially for ultra-thin, conformal films [N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1].

### Methods reserved for specific layers or features only
The evidence suggests that certain methods are used for specific layers or features rather than broadly for all metals:

- **ALD** is reserved for ultra-thin, conformal barrier films, caps, and etch-stop films in BEOL interconnects, where traditional PVD or PECVD may not reach [N1-F1].
- **CVD** is used for conformal contacts and for tungsten seed layers, while ALD is used for tantalum nitride and other barrier-like nanolaminates [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **EBE** appears to be used more selectively for thin-film metals such as aluminum and titanium-aluminum alloy, but the evidence is thinner and less central than for PVD and CVD [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### How device availability has changed with node scaling
The evidence reflects a clear trend: as nodes scale into sub-10nm and below, the need for **atomic-level uniformity, conformality, and nanoscale control** has increased, making **ALD** increasingly necessary for gate-all-around and other 3D structures [N1-R4][N1-F1][N1-R5]. At the same time, **PVD** remains ideal for metallic layers and planar or symmetric layers that require uniform stress and thickness control, while **CVD** bridges the gap between PVD and ALD by delivering excellent film quality and conformality for contacts and barrier-related materials [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].

So, the device availability picture is:
- **PVD** continues to be central and widely used for metallic layers.
- **CVD** becomes more important for conformal contacts and barrier-related materials.
- **ALD** becomes increasingly essential for the smallest geometries and most challenging barrier and cap layers.
- **EBE** and **MBE** are present but more specialized or limited in the provided evidence [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 2) Which metals are deposited by which device class?

### PVD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
The evidence identifies a broad set of metals deposited by PVD in semiconductor manufacturing:

- **aluminum**
- **copper**
- **titanium**
- **tungsten**
- **titanium tungsten (TiW)**
- **titanium aluminum (TiAl)**
- **nickel chromium (NiCr)**
- **silicon** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]

PVD is especially relevant for:
- **interconnects** [N2-F2]
- **barriers and adhesion layers** [N2-R4]
- **multi-material stacks** and alloys [N2-R1][N2-R5]

### CVD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
CVD is used for conformal and barrier-related deposition, with the evidence identifying:

- **tungsten**
- **cobalt**
- **cobalt silicide**
- **tungsten silicide**
- **tungsten nitride**
- **tantalum nitride** [N3-R5][N3-R2][N3-R1][N5-F3]

CVD is especially used for:
- **interconnects and contacts** [N3-R5]
- **capping and barrier layers** [N3-R5][N5-F3]
- **diffusion-barrier-related materials** [N3-R5][N3-R2]

### EBE-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
The evidence is thinner, but it does indicate that EBE is used for thin-film metals such as:

- **aluminum**
- **titanium-aluminum alloy**

It is also used for **atomized aluminum** in electronic materials and line substrates [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### ALD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
ALD is the clearest example of a method reserved for ultra-thin, conformal layers. The evidence identifies:

- **tantalum nitride (TaN)** [N5-F3][N5-R5]
- **tungsten nitride**
- **barrier films**
- **caps**
- **etch-stop films**
- **nanolaminates and ultra-thin films** [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R5]

### MBE-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
MBE is described as a high-quality crystalline thin-film technique, with evidence that it is used for:

- **tantalum** on semiconducting substrates
- **high-quality crystalline thin films** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]

The evidence is more limited than for PVD and CVD, so MBE appears to be more specialized than general-purpose.

---

## 3) Why each device is chosen for its metal

### Why a device is selected for purity, thickness, or uniformity needs
The evidence shows that the choice of deposition method is driven by the film’s required properties:

- **PVD** is selected because it produces **high-purity films** in a vacuum environment, which minimizes contamination [N7-R4]. This makes it ideal for metallic layers where purity matters, such as interconnects and adhesion layers [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is selected because it can deliver **excellent film quality** and is useful for conformal layers, especially in contacts and barrier-related structures [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].
- **ALD** is selected because it offers **angstrom-level thickness control** and can deposit **ultra-thin, conformal films** even in deep or narrow structures [N1-R4][N1-F1]. This is especially important for advanced-node barrier and cap layers.
- **EBE** is selected for thin-film applications such as **aluminum** and **titanium-aluminum alloy**, where atomization and thin-film quality matter [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Why a device is selected for adhesion or interface requirements
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes interface and adhesion requirements:

- **Titanium and titanium tungsten (Ti/TiW)** are specifically noted as critical elements in PVD processing that attach subsequent structures to device elements [N2-R4]. This means PVD is chosen when a good **adhesion layer** is needed.
- **CVD** is often used with an **adhesion/barrier layer** such as Ti/TiN, which improves the interface for subsequent deposition [N3-R5].
- **ALD tantalum nitride (TaN)** is used to improve adhesion between an underlying copper structure and overlying materials [N5-R4].
- **ALD** is chosen because its self-limiting surface chemistry allows films to grow one monolayer at a time, improving **interface uniformity** and **film continuity** in complex geometries [N1-F1].

### Why a device is selected for compatibility with advanced-node process steps
The evidence shows that the choice is also driven by the broader process flow:

- **PVD** is used when **metallic layers** and **planar or symmetric layers** are needed, and it is central to interconnect fabrication [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is used when **conformal contacts** or **barrier-related materials** are needed, especially in conjunction with adhesion layers [N3-R5].
- **ALD** is used when **nanoscale control**, **3D geometries**, and **ultra-thin conformal films** are required, making it indispensable for advanced-node BEOL processing [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **EBE** is used in thin-film applications where atomization and thin-film quality matter, though it appears more specialized [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- **MBE** is used for **high-quality crystalline thin films**, including tantalum on semiconducting substrates, where crystal quality matters more than general metal-metal deposition [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 4) Advanced-node metal layer roles and deposition-method fit

### Which metal layers are used in interconnects, barriers, capping, or diffusion layers?
The evidence identifies several key roles:

- **Interconnects**: PVD is used for metallic interconnects [N2-F2]. CVD is used for tungsten seed layers and contacts [N3-R5]. ALD is used for diffusion barriers, caps, and etch-stop films in BEOL [N1-F1].
- **Barriers**: PVD provides titanium and titanium tungsten as adhesion/barrier layers [N2-R4]. CVD is used alongside barrier layers such as Ti/TiN [N3-R5]. ALD tantalum nitride improves adhesion between copper structures and overlying materials [N5-R4].
- **Capping and etch-stop**: ALD is used for caps and etch-stop films where conformality is critical [N1-F1].
- **Diffusion barriers**: CVD and ALD are both used for diffusion barriers, including tungsten nitride and tantalum nitride [N3-R5][N5-F3].

### How geometry and thickness requirements shape the choice of deposition method
The evidence clearly shows that geometry and thickness are central to method selection:

- **PVD** is good for metallic layers but relatively poor in step coverage for deep trenches or high-aspect-ratio structures [N7-R1].
- **CVD** is better for conformal layers, especially tungsten in contacts and for barrier-related materials [N3-R5][N7-R2].
- **ALD** is the best fit for **ultra-thin**, **conformal**, and **deep/narrow structures**, because its sequential surface reactions allow uniform deposition even in difficult geometries [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **EBE** is used where thin-film quality matters, but it is not as central to the general picture as PVD and CVD [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### How the same layer may use multiple methods in different process steps
The evidence supports the idea that a single layer can involve multiple methods in different steps. For example:

- **CVD** may be used for a **seed layer or contact fill**, while **ALD** is used for a **barrier or cap layer** [N3-R5][N1-F1].
- **PVD** may be used for the **base metallic layer**, while **CVD** or **ALD** is used for the **adhesion/barrier or diffusion barrier** [N2-R4][N3-R5][N5-R4].

This hybrid approach reflects the need to balance **purity, conformality, adhesion, and process compatibility** across the same layer.

---

## 5) Bottom line

In advanced-node chip manufacturing, the metal-film deposition landscape is shaped by the following:

| Device        | Metals typically deposited           | Layer roles and why it is chosen                                                                 | Best fit for geometry/thickness                          |
|---------------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| **PVD**       | Al, Cu, Ti, W, TiW, TiAl, NiCr     | Interconnects, adhesion/barriers, multi-material stacks; high purity and uniformity [N2-R1][N2-F2] | Planar or symmetric layers; metallic interconnects [N2-R4] |
| **CVD**       | W, Co, CoSi, WSi, WxNy, TaNx       | Contacts, barrier-related materials, conformal films [N3-R5][N5-F3]                               | Conformal contacts and barrier-related layers [N3-R5]     |

## Integrated final answer: which devices are used, which metals they deposit, and why

In advanced-node chip manufacturing, the metal-film deposition process is not a one-size-fits-all recipe. Instead, it is a carefully selected combination of deposition methods tailored to the metal, layer role, geometry, and process step. Based on the provided branch reports, the most relevant methods in advanced-node metal-layer processing are:

- **physical vapor deposition (PVD)**
- **chemical vapor deposition (CVD)**
- **atomic layer deposition (ALD)**
- **electron beam evaporation (EBE)**
- **molecular beam epitaxy (MBE)**

The evidence also suggests that **MBE** is more specialized and less central to general metal-metal deposition in the provided sources, while **EBE** is present but thinner in the evidence than PVD and CVD [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-R5][N5-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 1) Which devices are actually used in advanced-node chip manufacturing?

### Commonly used methods
The branch reports indicate that **PVD, CVD, and ALD** are the most commonly used in advanced-node metal-layer processing [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1].

- **PVD** is described as the cornerstone technique for semiconductor manufacturing and especially relevant for metallic layers [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is presented as complementary to PVD and useful where conformality and film quality matter [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].
- **ALD** is described as the most advanced deposition method in the market and indispensable for managing advanced-node challenges, especially for ultra-thin, conformal films [N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1].

### Methods reserved for specific layers or features only
The evidence suggests that certain methods are used for specific layers or features rather than broadly for all metals:

- **ALD** is reserved for ultra-thin, conformal barrier films, caps, and etch-stop films in BEOL interconnects, where traditional PVD or PECVD may not reach [N1-F1].
- **CVD** is used for conformal contacts and for tungsten seed layers, while ALD is used for tantalum nitride and other barrier-like nanolaminates [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **EBE** appears to be used more selectively for thin-film metals such as aluminum and titanium-aluminum alloy, but the evidence is thinner and less central than for PVD and CVD [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### How device availability has changed with node scaling
The evidence reflects a clear trend: as nodes scale into sub-10nm and below, the need for **atomic-level uniformity, conformality, and nanoscale control** has increased, making **ALD** increasingly necessary for gate-all-around and other 3D structures [N1-R4][N1-F1][N1-R5]. At the same time, **PVD** remains ideal for metallic layers and planar or symmetric layers that require uniform stress and thickness control, while **CVD** bridges the gap between PVD and ALD by delivering excellent film quality and conformality for contacts and barrier-related materials [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].

So, the device availability picture is:
- **PVD** continues to be central and widely used for metallic layers.
- **CVD** becomes more important for conformal contacts and barrier-related materials.
- **ALD** becomes increasingly essential for the smallest geometries and most challenging barrier and cap layers.
- **EBE** and **MBE** are present but more specialized or limited in the provided evidence [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 2) Which metals are deposited by which device class?

### PVD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
The evidence identifies a broad set of metals deposited by PVD in semiconductor manufacturing:

- **aluminum**
- **copper**
- **titanium**
- **tungsten**
- **titanium tungsten (TiW)**
- **titanium aluminum (TiAl)**
- **nickel chromium (NiCr)**
- **silicon** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]

PVD is especially relevant for:
- **interconnects** [N2-F2]
- **barriers and adhesion layers** [N2-R4]
- **multi-material stacks** and alloys [N2-R1][N2-R5]

### CVD-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
CVD is used for conformal and barrier-related deposition, with the evidence identifying:

- **tungsten**
- **cobalt**
- **cobalt silicide**
- **tungsten silicide**
- **tungsten nitride**
- **tantalum nitride** [N3-R5][N3-R2][N3-R1][N5-F3]

CVD is especially used for:
- **interconnects and contacts** [N3-R5]
- **capping and barrier layers** [N3-R5][N5-F3]
- **diffusion-barrier-related materials** [N3-R5][N3-R2]

### EBE-deposited metals and their typical layer roles
The evidence is thinner, but it does indicate that EBE is used for thin-film metals such as:

- **aluminum**
- **titanium-aluminum alloy**

It is also used for **atomized aluminum** in electronic materials and line substrates [N4-R2][N4-R5].

The evidence is more limited than for PVD and CVD, so MBE appears to be more specialized than general-purpose.

## 3) Why each device is chosen for its metal

### Why a device is selected for purity, thickness, or uniformity needs
The evidence shows that the choice of deposition method is driven by the film’s required properties:

- **PVD** is selected because it produces **high-purity films** in a vacuum environment, which minimizes contamination [N7-R4]. This makes it ideal for metallic layers where purity matters, such as interconnects and adhesion layers [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is selected because it can deliver **excellent film quality** and is useful for conformal layers, especially in contacts and barrier-related structures [N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].
- **ALD** is selected because it offers **angstrom-level thickness control** and can deposit **ultra-thin, conformal films** even in deep or narrow structures [N1-R4][N1-F1]. This is especially important for advanced-node barrier and cap layers.
- **EBE** is selected for thin-film applications such as **aluminum** and **titanium-aluminum alloy**, where atomization and thin-film quality matter [N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Why a device is selected for adhesion or interface requirements
The evidence repeatedly emphasizes interface and adhesion requirements:

- **Titanium and titanium tungsten (Ti/TiW)** are specifically noted as critical elements in PVD processing that attach subsequent structures to device elements [N2-R4]. This means PVD is chosen when a good **adhesion layer** is needed.
- **CVD** is often used with an **adhesion/barrier layer** such as Ti/TiN, which improves the interface for subsequent deposition [N3-R5].
- **ALD tantalum nitride (TaN)** is used to improve adhesion between an underlying copper structure and overlying materials [N5-R4].
- **ALD** is chosen because its self-limiting surface chemistry allows films to grow one monolayer at a time, improving **interface uniformity** and **film continuity** in complex geometries [N1-F1].

### Why a device is selected for compatibility with advanced-node process steps
The evidence shows that the choice is also driven by the broader process flow:

- **PVD** is used when **metallic layers** and **planar or symmetric layers** are needed, and it is central to interconnect fabrication [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **CVD** is used when **conformal contacts** or **barrier-related materials** are needed, especially in conjunction with adhesion layers [N3-R5].
- **ALD** is used when **nanoscale control**, **3D geometries**, and **ultra-thin conformal films** are required, making it indispensable for advanced-node BEOL processing [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **EBE** is used in thin-film applications where atomization and thin-film quality matter, though it appears more specialized [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- **MBE** is used for **high-quality crystalline thin films**, including tantalum on semiconducting substrates, where crystal quality matters more than general metal-metal deposition [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

## 4) Advanced-node metal layer roles and deposition-method fit

- **Capping and etch-stop**: ALD is used for caps and etch-stop films where conformality is critical [N1-F1].

The evidence clearly shows that geometry and thickness are central to method selection:

- **PVD** is good for metallic layers but relatively poor in step coverage for deep trenches or high-aspect-ratio structures [N7-R1].
- **CVD** is better for conformal layers, especially tungsten in contacts and for barrier-related materials [N3-R5][N7-R2].

- **EBE** is used where thin-film quality matters, but it is not as central to the general picture as PVD and CVD [N4-R2][N4-R5].

The evidence supports the idea that a single layer can involve multiple methods in different steps. For example:

- **CVD** may be used for a **seed layer or contact fill**, while **ALD** is used for a **barrier or cap layer** [N3-R5][N1-F1].
